claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, exposure to predatory wasps leads to inheritance of a predisposition for ethanol-rich food for five generations.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, exposure to predatory wasps leads to inheritance of a predisposition for ethanol-rich food for five generations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ethanol preference persisting through F5 generation as shown in Figure 1b and described in the Results section.

claim: Inhibition of Neuropeptide-F (NPF) activates germline caspases required for transgenerational ethanol preference.
source: Inhibition of Neuropeptide-F (NPF) activates germline caspases required for transgenerational ethanol preference.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing NPF knockdown induces germline apoptosis and that germline caspase knockdown prevents inheritance of ethanol preference.

claim: Inheritance of low NPF expression in specific regions of F1 brains is required for the transmission of ethanol preference.
source: Further, inheritance of low NPF expression in specific regions of F1 brains is required for the transmission of this food preference
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced NPF protein levels in the fan shaped body of F1 and F2 flies (Figure 4b).

claim: A maternally derived NPF locus is necessary for transgenerational inheritance of ethanol preference.
source: a maternally derived NPF locus is necessary for this phenomenon, implicating a maternal epigenetic mechanism of NPF-repression.
evidence: Supported by compound chromosome experiments and NPF deficiency experiments showing maternal NPF locus is required (Figure 5d, 5f).

claim: Children conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter had higher rates of obesity and diabetes.
source: Children conceived in the Netherlands during the World War II blockade, and ensuing famine, had higher rates of obesity and diabetes (Heijmans et al., 2008; Schulz, 2010; Stein et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on the Dutch Hunger Winter.

claim: Risk factors for children of Holocaust survivors have been linked to methylation state of the glucocorticoid receptor promoter.
source: Further, risk factors for children of Holocaust survivors, such as reduced cortisol sensitivity, have been linked to methylation state of the glucocorticoid receptor promoter, and increased methylation in offspring has been associated with paternal diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder (Yehuda et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on Holocaust survivors.

claim: Male mice trained to associate fear with an odor transmitted sensitivity of this odor to their sons.
source: For example, male mice trained to associate fear with an odor, transmitted sensitivity of this odor to their sons. In this instance, researchers concluded that offspring possessed an increased abundance of sensory neurons specific to the same odor their fathers were trained to fear (Dias and Ressler, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on olfactory fear conditioning in mice.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster females, when cohabitated with endoparasitoid wasps, shift to prefer ethanol food as an egglaying substrate.
source: Drosophila melanogaster females, when cohabitated with endoparasitoid wasps, shift to prefer ethanol food as an egglaying substrate, where ethanol food protects Drosophila larvae from wasp infection (Kacsoh et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Ethanol preference in D. melanogaster is linked to a decrease in Neuropeptide F (NPF) in the female brain.
source: Ethanol preference in D. melanogaster is linked to a decrease in Neuropeptide F (NPF) in the female brain (Kacsoh et al., 2013), consistent with previous work on NPF (Shohat-Ophir et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: NPY modulation governs ethanol consumption in rats.
source: NPY modulation governs ethanol consumption in rats (Thiele et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on NPY in rats.

claim: NPY is implicated in human alcohol abuse disorders.
source: and is implicated in human alcohol abuse disorders (Mayfield et al., 2002; Mottagui-Tabar et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on NPY in human alcohol disorders.

claim: Wasp-exposed Canton-S flies lay approximately 94% of their eggs on ethanol food.
source: Wasp-exposed Canton-S flies lay approximately 94% of their eggs on ethanol food (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Ethanol preference persists in F1 offspring despite never having direct interaction with wasps.
source: This behavior persists in their offspring despite the F1 generation never having direct interaction with wasps (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Ethanol preference in F1 was less potent, with 73% of the eggs laid on ethanol food.
source: Ethanol preference in F1 was less potent, with 73% of the eggs laid on ethanol food (p=8.6e−7, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance reported.

claim: Inherited ethanol preference persisted for five generations, gradually reverting back to the mock exposed baseline.
source: Remarkably, this inherited ethanol preference persisted for five generations, gradually reverting back to the mock exposed baseline (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Inheritance of ethanol preference was replicated in Oregon R (OR) strain.
source: These observations were replicated in an additional wild type Oregon R (OR) strain (Supplementary file 2), suggesting that the phenomenon is not specific to a particular genetic aberration or background.
evidence: Supported by experimental replication data in a different genetic background.

claim: Inheritance of ethanol preference is not a permanent germline change, but rather it is a reversible trait.
source: This indicates that inheritance of ethanol preference is not a permanent germline change, but rather it is a reversible trait.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ethanol preference decays over generations and returns to baseline by F6.

claim: Long-term memory mutant Orb2ΔQ produced offspring with an ethanol preference when embryo collection was conducted in the presence of wasps.
source: The long-term memory mutant Orb2ΔQ produced offspring with an ethanol preference when the embryo collection for the F1 generation was conducted in the presence of wasps, but this ethanol preference was greatly reduced in offspring collected post-wasp exposure (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Ethanol preference was greatly reduced in Orb2ΔQ offspring collected post-wasp exposure.
source: The long-term memory mutant Orb2ΔQ produced offspring with an ethanol preference when the embryo collection for the F1 generation was conducted in the presence of wasps, but this ethanol preference was greatly reduced in offspring collected post-wasp exposure (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Similar results were found for the memory mutant amn1.
source: Similar results were found for the memory mutant amn1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Legacy flies collected during wasp exposure from conditional Orb2 knockdown flies exhibited an ethanol preference.
source: Legacy flies collected during the wasp exposure and subsequently tested did exhibit an ethanol preference (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Legacy flies from parental RU486 treatment collected post-wasp exposure did not display an ethanol preference.
source: However, legacy flies from the parental RU486 treatment collected post-wasp exposure did not display an ethanol preference.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional Orb2 knockdown experiments.

claim: Functional long-term memory is not a compulsory requirement to generate ethanol-preferring offspring.
source: These data provide insight in two ways: First, functional long-term memory is not a compulsory requirement to generate ethanol-preferring offspring.
evidence: Inferred from memory mutant experiments showing offspring can inherit ethanol preference when collected during wasp exposure.

claim: Intact long-term memory is not required to inherit ethanol preference.
source: Second, the mutant data suggests that intact long-term memory is not required to inherit ethanol preference.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with memory mutants and conditional knockdown.

claim: The neuronal signaling is different for maintained ethanol preference in the F0 and F1 flies.
source: Given that ethanol preference in the absence of wasps is long-term memory dependent, this experiment reveals that the neuronal signaling is different for maintained ethanol preference in the F0 and F1 flies (Bozler et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from differences in memory requirements between F0 and F1 generations, with citation to previous work.

claim: Following wasp exposure, F0 flies have an ethanol preference that persists for more than a week, returning to baseline after ten days.
source: We confirmed previous findings, where, following a wasp exposure, F0 flies have an ethanol preference that persists for more than a week, returning to baseline after ten days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Brood two (collected ten days post wasp exposure) did not display an inherited ethanol preference.
source: Brood two did not display an inherited ethanol preference, suggesting that wasp exposure does not inflict a permanent change in the F0 germline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Wasp exposure does not inflict a permanent change in the F0 germline.
source: Brood two did not display an inherited ethanol preference, suggesting that wasp exposure does not inflict a permanent change in the F0 germline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that offspring collected after F0 ethanol preference has decayed do not inherit the behavior.

claim: Inherited ethanol preference can be enhanced with successive generations of wasp exposure.
source: We found that inherited ethanol preference can be enhanced with successive generations of wasp exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The enhancing effect did not repeat when nonconsecutive generations were repeatedly exposed to wasps.
source: This trend did not repeat when nonconsecutive generations were repeatedly exposed to wasps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The enhancing effect observed in successive exposures is time sensitive and may be linked to the ethanol preference of the parental flies.
source: This suggests that the enhancing effect observed in the successive exposures is time sensitive and may be linked to the ethanol preference of the parental flies.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on differences between successive and non-consecutive exposure experiments.

claim: Male F1 legacy flies mated to naïve females produced offspring (F2) with an ethanol preference.
source: Male F1 legacy flies, mated to naïve females produced offspring (F2) with an ethanol preference (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: 14–16 day old F1 flies displayed an ethanol preference.
source: Additionally, 14–16 day old F1 flies displayed an ethanol preference, demonstrating that F1 flies do not have an ethanol preference decay curve similar to that of the F0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: F1 flies do not have an ethanol preference decay curve similar to that of the F0.
source: Additionally, 14–16 day old F1 flies displayed an ethanol preference, demonstrating that F1 flies do not have an ethanol preference decay curve similar to that of the F0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that aged F1 flies maintain ethanol preference.

claim: Analysis of the F0 data detected 98 differentially expressed transcripts (15 down and 83 up).
source: Analysis of the F0 data detected 98 differentially expressed transcripts (15 down and 83 up) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: F1 and F2 heads showed very few differentially expressed transcripts, 4 and 5 transcripts respectively.
source: F1 and F2 heads showed very few differentially expressed transcripts, 4 and 5 transcripts respectively.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: No transcript was shared between F0, F1, and F2 groups among differentially expressed transcripts.
source: Of the differentially expressed transcripts, no transcript was shared between groups.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Wasp exposure results in global transcriptional changes in the female head, but this does not hold true for subsequent generations.
source: These data indicate that although wasp exposure itself results in global transcriptional changes in the female head, this observation does not hold true for the subsequent generations.
evidence: Inferred from RNA sequencing data showing many changes in F0 but few in F1 and F2.

claim: Mid-oogenesis germline apoptosis (stage 7–8 oocytes) is triggered upon wasp exposure.
source: Mid-oogenesis germline apoptosis (stage 7–8 oocytes) is triggered upon wasp exposure (Figure 2a) (Kacsoh et al., 2018b; Kacsoh et al., 2018a; Kacsoh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and citations to previous work.

claim: Wasp-induced germline apoptosis is not heritable like the ethanol preference behavior.
source: However, this wasp response is not heritable like the ethanol preference behavior, and F1 females do not exhibit germline apoptosis (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: F1 females do not exhibit germline apoptosis.
source: However, this wasp response is not heritable like the ethanol preference behavior, and F1 females do not exhibit germline apoptosis (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Maternal germline knockdown of Dcp-1 produces offspring without an ethanol preference, regardless of parental treatment.
source: Nevertheless, maternal germline knockdown of the effector caspases Dcp-1 and drice (maternal-αtubulin-Gal4 > UAS-Dcp-1[RNAi], and maternal-αtubulin-Gal4 > UAS-Drice[RNAi] respectively) produce offspring without an ethanol preference, regardless of parental treatment (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Maternal germline knockdown of drice produces offspring without an ethanol preference, regardless of parental treatment.
source: Nevertheless, maternal germline knockdown of the effector caspases Dcp-1 and drice (maternal-αtubulin-Gal4 > UAS-Dcp-1[RNAi], and maternal-αtubulin-Gal4 > UAS-Drice[RNAi] respectively) produce offspring without an ethanol preference, regardless of parental treatment (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Protein-starvation triggers germline apoptosis similar to wasp exposure.
source: Although protein-starvation triggers germline apoptosis similar to wasp exposure (Figure 2b)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Offspring from mothers with starvation-induced apoptosis do not inherit an ethanol preference.
source: offspring from mothers with starvation-induced apoptosis do not inherit an ethanol preference (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Germline apoptosis in and of itself is not sufficient for inheritance of ethanol preference.
source: This indicates that germline apoptosis in and of itself is not sufficient for inheritance of ethanol preference.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that protein starvation causes apoptosis but not inherited ethanol preference.

claim: NPF levels decrease in the fan shaped body of female fly brains following wasp exposure.
source: NPF is known to play a role in food seeking, ethanol consumption, and numerous other reward pathways, and NPF levels decrease in the fan shaped body of female fly brains following wasp exposure (Kacsoh et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Overexpression of NPF inhibits ethanol preference even in the presence of wasps.
source: Even in the presence of wasps, overexpression of NPF (NPF-Gal4 >UAS NPF) inhibits ethanol preference
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Knockdown of NPF is sufficient to induce ethanol preference in the absence of wasps.
source: while in the absence of wasps, knockdown of NPF (NPF-Gal4 >UAS-NPF[RNAi]) is sufficient to induce the ethanol preference behavior (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: NPF knockdown induces mid-oogenesis apoptosis in the absence of wasps.
source: Strikingly, NPF knockdown induces mid-oogenesis apoptosis in the absence of wasps (Figure 3b)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Overexpression of NPF results in no elevation in germline apoptosis even in the presence of wasps.
source: while overexpression of NPF results in no elevation in germline apoptosis even in the presence of wasps (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: NPF-receptor (NPFR) knockdown in neurons alone leads to significantly elevated levels of apoptosis (28%).
source: Similarly, NPF-receptor (NPFR) knockdown in neurons (Elav-Gal4 >UAS-NPFR[RNAi]) alone leads to significantly elevated levels of apoptosis (28%, when compared to parental line controls p=6.2e−4 and 1.5e−4)
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical significance reported.

claim: NPFR knockdown effect on apoptosis is enhanced with wasp exposure (61%).
source: and this effect is enhanced with wasp exposure (61%, p=7.0e−4) (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c with statistical significance.

claim: NPF-triggered changes link ethanol preference behavior and mid-oogenesis apoptosis in F0 females.
source: Taken together these observations link ethanol preference behavior and mid-oogenesis apoptosis in the F0 females, where both processes are likely caused by changes in NPF and NPFR signaling.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing NPF modulates both behaviors.

claim: Legacy flies from mothers with NPF knockdown exhibit ethanol preference, even in the absence of wasp exposure.
source: Legacy flies from mothers with NPF knockdown exhibit ethanol preference, even in the absence of wasp exposure (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inherited ethanol preference is enhanced when parental NPF knockdown flies are exposed to wasps.
source: Inherited ethanol preference is enhanced when the parental NPF knockdown flies are exposed to wasps (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: NPF overexpression in F0 mothers exposed to wasps produced offspring lacking the ethanol preference.
source: By contrast, NPF overexpression in F0 mothers exposed to wasps produced offspring lacking the ethanol preference (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Maternal NPFR knockdown produces offspring with an ethanol preference compared to unexposed control lines.
source: NPFR knockdown experiments mirror these findings: Maternal NPFR knockdown produces offspring with an ethanol preference compared to unexposed control lines
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The effect of maternal NPFR knockdown on offspring ethanol preference is enhanced when paired with wasp exposure.
source: again this effect is enhanced when NPFR knockdown is paired with wasp exposure (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Overexpression of NPF in F1 flies blocks ethanol preference in the exposed F1 legacy group.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of NPF in F1 flies blocks ethanol preference in the exposed F1 legacy group (Figure 3f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: F1 legacy flies inherit NPF in a repressed or low expression state.
source: raising the possibility that F1 legacy flies inherit NPF in a repressed or low expression state.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observation that NPF overexpression can rescue the inherited phenotype.

claim: Global changes in NPF RNA were not detected in either the F0 or F1 female heads.
source: We therefore hypothesized that regulation or depression of NPF might be a means of this behavioral inheritance. Global changes in NPF RNA were not detected in either the F0 or F1 female heads (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NPF protein levels were significantly reduced in the fan shaped body of F0, F1, and F2 (two-generations exposed) flies.
source: NPF protein levels measured through immunofluorescence were significantly reduced in the fan shaped body of F0, F1, and F2 (two-generations exposed) flies (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: NPF was not reduced in all regions of the F1 and F2 brains.
source: We note that NPF was not reduced in all regions of the F1 and F2 brains, as intensity of P1 neurons was not reduced in either the F1 or F2 flies
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Significant reduction of NPF was observed in P1 neurons of F0 flies.
source: although significant reduction was observed in P1 neurons of F0 flies (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: F1 offspring from an exclusively maternal wasp exposure inherit ethanol preference.
source: Interestingly, F1 offspring from an exclusively maternal wasp exposure inherit ethanol preference, while F1 offspring from an exclusively paternal exposure did not (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: F1 offspring from an exclusively paternal wasp exposure did not inherit ethanol preference.
source: Interestingly, F1 offspring from an exclusively maternal wasp exposure inherit ethanol preference, while F1 offspring from an exclusively paternal exposure did not (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There is a key difference between the F0 males and the F1 males in transmitting ethanol preference.
source: Importantly, this demonstrates a key difference between the F0 males and the F1 males, and it may point to an 'activation phase' and 'maintenance phase' of the epigenetic program.
evidence: Inferred from differences in paternal transmission between F0 and F1 generations.

claim: Female flies require sight to induce a behavioral response to wasp exposure.
source: We have previously reported that female flies require sight to induce a behavioral response to wasp exposure (Kacsoh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Blind female flies (ninaB1; UAS-ninaB) mated to CS males did not produce offspring with an ethanol preference.
source: In further support of the maternal contribution to the inheritance of ethanol preference, blind female flies (ninaB1; UAS-ninaB) mated to CS males did not produce offspring with an ethanol preference (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Blind fathers mated to CS females did generate ethanol-preferring offspring following a wasp exposure.
source: In the reciprocal experiment, blind fathers mated to CS females did generate ethanol-preferring offspring following a wasp exposure (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Chromosome-II fusion flies had similar results when inheriting exclusively maternal or paternal Chromosome-II elements.
source: Chromosome-II fusion flies had similar results when inheriting exclusively maternal or paternal Chromosome-II elements (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Chromosome-III fusion flies had inheritance of ethanol preference when receiving both copies of Chromosome-III maternally.
source: Chromosome-III fusion flies also had inheritance of ethanol preference when receiving both copies of Chromosome-III maternally.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Flies with both copies of Chromosome-III from their fathers failed to inherit an ethanol preference.
source: However, flies with both copies of Chromosome-III from their fathers failed to inherit an ethanol preference (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Some element on Chromosome-III must be inherited from wasp-exposed mothers in order for ethanol preference behavior to be passed on to F1 legacy flies.
source: This observation has at least three implications: Most importantly, this indicates that some element on Chromosome-III must be inherited from wasp-exposed mothers in order for ethanol preference behavior to be passed on to F1 legacy flies.
evidence: Inferred from compound chromosome experiments showing maternal Chromosome-III is required.

claim: Maternal copies of the Chromosome-X, Chromosome-II or cytoplasmic factors, if important, are not sufficient for inheritance of ethanol preference.
source: This also suggests that maternal copies of the Chromosome-X, Chromosome-II or cytoplasmic factors, if important, are not sufficient for inheritance of ethanol preference.
evidence: Inferred from compound chromosome experiments showing Chromosome-III is necessary.

claim: Exclusion of maternal chromosomes itself does not generally interfere with transgenerational inheritance.
source: Lastly, that oocytes giving rise to eggs with zero copies of maternal Chromosome-II still confer ethanol preference, indicates that exclusion of maternal chromosomes itself does not generally interfere with transgenerational inheritance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that paternal Chromosome-II is sufficient for inheritance.

claim: Legacy F1 flies from exposed mothers inheriting a wild-type NPF on a balancer chromosome exhibited a strong preference for ethanol.
source: Legacy F1 flies from exposed mothers inheriting a wild-type NPF on a balancer chromosome exhibited a strong preference for ethanol, suggesting that multiple rearrangements, deletions and mutations of a balancer Chromosome-III are not sufficient to prevent ethanol preference in F1 flies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Multiple rearrangements, deletions and mutations of a balancer Chromosome-III are not sufficient to prevent ethanol preference in F1 flies.
source: Legacy F1 flies from exposed mothers inheriting a wild-type NPF on a balancer chromosome exhibited a strong preference for ethanol, suggesting that multiple rearrangements, deletions and mutations of a balancer Chromosome-III are not sufficient to prevent ethanol preference in F1 flies.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that balancer chromosomes with intact NPF support inheritance.

claim: Legacy F1 flies from exposed mothers inheriting a Chromosome-III deletion of the NPF gene region do not inherit any preference for ethanol.
source: By contrast, legacy F1 flies from exposed mothers inheriting a Chromosome-III deletion of the NPF gene region do not inherit any preference for ethanol (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Two different Chromosome-III deletions at the NPF locus prevent inheritance of ethanol preference.
source: This was true for two different Chromosome-III deletions at the NPF locus
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: A Chromosome-III deletion that does not disrupt the NPF gene had no effect on inheritance of ethanol preference.
source: whereas a Chromosome-III deletion that does not disrupt the NPF gene had no effect (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Paternally inherited Chromosome-III deletions were not sufficient to prevent ethanol preference in F1 flies.
source: Paternally inherited Chromosome-III deletions were not sufficient to prevent ethanol preference in F1 flies (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The ethanol preference behavior is heritable but modifiable and responsive to environmental cues.
source: Indeed, it would appear that animals are bound to their ancestors in a way that some might consider Lamarckian (Galloway and Etterson, 2007; Herman and Sultan, 2011; J. Marshall and Uller, 2007). The ethanol preference we observed in this study is heritable but modifiable and responsive to environmental cues, as it can be enhanced or decay across generations.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of ethanol preference across generations with citations to relevant literature.

claim: There is an ultimate return to pre-wasp exposed state by the F6 generation.
source: Our data suggest that there is an ultimate return to pre-wasp exposed state by the F6 generation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ethanol preference returns to baseline by F6.

claim: No priming or enhancement effect was detected in the F8 generation following a second wasp exposure.
source: Not only does the ethanol preference behavior revert to unexposed levels, but we also detected no priming or enhancement effect in the F8 generation following a second wasp exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The initiation of the epigenetic program in the founding generation (F0) is maternal in nature.
source: Inheritance of ethanol preference requires several factors: We found that the initiation of the epigenetic program in the founding generation (F0) is maternal in nature, and requires effector caspases in the female germline.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing maternal exposure is required and germline caspases are necessary.

claim: Initiation of the epigenetic program requires effector caspases in the female germline.
source: Inheritance of ethanol preference requires several factors: We found that the initiation of the epigenetic program in the founding generation (F0) is maternal in nature, and requires effector caspases in the female germline.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing caspase knockdown prevents inheritance.

claim: Both male and female progeny (F1) are able to pass on ethanol preference to their offspring.
source: Both male and female progeny (F1) are able to pass on ethanol preference to their offspring.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing F1 males can transmit the phenotype.

claim: The lack of female germline apoptosis and paternal ability to confer ethanol preference points to a caspase-independent maintenance mechanism.
source: Although, it is possible that the F1 generation requires germline effector caspases for the transmission of the ethanol preference, the lack of female germline apoptosis and paternal ability to confer this behavior points to a caspase-independent maintenance mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from observations that F1 females lack apoptosis but can still transmit the phenotype, and F1 males can also transmit.

claim: Maternal imprinting of the NPF locus or nearby regions has a dominant effect, leading to the possibility that the F1 paternal locus is imprinted in trans.
source: Maternal imprinting of the NPF locus or nearby regions has a dominant effect, leading to the possibility that the F1 paternal locus is imprinted in trans.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on maternal NPF locus requirement and dominant inheritance pattern.

claim: NPF and its mammalian homolog NPY have conserved signaling functions in drug and alcohol disorders.
source: Given the conserved signaling functions of NPF and its mammalian NPY homolog in drug and alcohol disorders, these observations raise the intriguing possibility of NPY-related transgenerational effects in humans.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about NPF/NPY function.

claim: These observations raise the intriguing possibility of NPY-related transgenerational effects in humans.
source: Given the conserved signaling functions of NPF and its mammalian NPY homolog in drug and alcohol disorders, these observations raise the intriguing possibility of NPY-related transgenerational effects in humans.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation from Drosophila findings to potential human implications.

claim: Ethanol food protects Drosophila larvae from wasp infection.
source: Drosophila melanogaster females, when cohabitated with endoparasitoid wasps, shift to prefer ethanol food as an egglaying substrate, where ethanol food protects Drosophila larvae from wasp infection (Kacsoh et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Drosophila suzukii shifts egglaying preference to food with atropine, giving its progeny protection against wasps.
source: Drosophila suzukii similarly shifts egglaying preference to food with atropine, giving its progeny protection against wasps (Poyet et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on D. suzukii.

claim: NPF signaling is rewarding.
source: This behavioral output is believed to be a consequence of the NPF/NPY role in the rewards pathway, with NPF signaling being rewarding (Desai et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on NPF reward signaling.

claim: NPF activity is considered representative of the motivational state of the fly.
source: NPF activity is considered representative of the motivational state of the fly (Krashes et al., 2009; Landayan and Wolf, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on NPF and motivation.

claim: Stressful experiences regulate NPY/NPF levels, providing a link between environmental cues and NPF/NPY signaling.
source: Several recent studies also have shown that 'stressful' experiences regulate NPY/NPF levels, providing a link between environmental cues and NPF/NPY signaling (Broqua et al., 1995; Sah et al., 2009; Shohat-Ophir et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on stress and NPY/NPF.

claim: Environmental enrichment activities can ameliorate behavioral defects of mutant mice defective in long-term potentiation and memory.
source: Similarly, environmental enrichment activities can ameliorate behavioral defects of mutant mice defective in long-term potentiation and memory. This behavioral rescue is heritable to the next generation through the activation of an otherwise latent p38 signaling cascade (Arai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on environmental enrichment in mice.

claim: This behavioral rescue is heritable to the next generation through the activation of an otherwise latent p38 signaling cascade.
source: This behavioral rescue is heritable to the next generation through the activation of an otherwise latent p38 signaling cascade (Arai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Parental exposure to toxins and nutritional challenges can change germline information, affecting growth and metabolism of future generations.
source: Parental exposure to toxins and nutritional challenges also can change germline information, affecting growth and metabolism of future generations (Carone et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016; Skinner et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on parental exposures.

claim: The Figitid larval endoparasitoid Leptopilina heterotoma (strain Lh14) was used in the experiments.
source: The Figitid larval endoparasitoid Leptopilina heterotoma (strain Lh14) was used.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: Wasps aged 3–7 days post eclosion were used for all infections and experiments.
source: Wasps aged 3–7 days post eclosion were used for all infections and experiments, and were never reused for experiments.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: The wasp exposure period lasted for four days.
source: Mature adult flies were used for wasp exposures: 40 female flies, 10 male flies, and 20 female Lh14 (Leptopilina heterotoma) wasps were placed in a vial with cornmeal-molasses media. This cohabitation (wasp exposure period) lasted for four days.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: Control food was hydrated entirely with distilled water, whereas ethanol food was prepared with distilled water and a final addition of 95% ethanol to create food with 6% ethanol by volume.
source: Control food was hydrated entirely with distilled water, where as ethanol food was prepared with distilled water and a final addition of 95% ethanol to the top of the prepared food, creating a food with 6% ethanol by volume.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: Baseline ethanol preference is highly variable depending on environmental conditions.
source: It is critical to note that baseline ethanol preference is highly variable depending on environmental conditions.
evidence: Direct observation from experimental experience.

claim: All ethanol oviposition assays were conducted in an environmentally controlled room at 25°C, approximately 30% humidity (±10%) with overhead lighting and a 12 hr light/dark cycle.
source: Key factors are temperature and humidity, all ethanol oviposition assays were conducted in an environmentally controlled room at 25°C, approximately 30% humidity (±10%) with overhead lighting and a 12 hr light/dark cycle.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: Baseline ethanol preference varies day-to-day despite environmental controls.
source: Despite these controls, baseline ethanol preference varies day-to-day.
evidence: Direct observation from experimental experience.

claim: All groups for direct comparison were tested at the same time to control for day-to-day variation.
source: For this reason, all groups for direct comparison (used in statistical tests) were tested at the same time.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design rationale.

claim: Apoptosis was scored based on the morphology of the nurse cell DNA.
source: Samples were stained with DAPI and apoptosis was scored based on the morphology of the nurse cell DNA.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: A researcher blinded to the genotype and treatment group of the samples performed the apoptosis scoring.
source: A researcher blinded to the genotype and treatment group of the samples performed the scoring.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods to reduce bias.

claim: The NPF antibody was generated in a rabbit to the full length NPF peptide.
source: Antibody to neuropeptide F was generated in a rabbit to the full length NPF peptide: C-Ahx-SNSRPPRKNDVNTMADAYKFLQDLDTYYGDRARVRFamide.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods.

claim: Anti-NPF signal has clear overlap with the NPF-Gal4 driving the cd8-GFP reporter.
source: Anti-NPF signal has clear overlap with the NPF-Gal4 driving the cd8-GFP reporter (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The fan shaped body has previously been implicated in ethanol preference.
source: The fan shaped body has previously been implicated in ethanol preference, and therefore, was a focus in this experiment (Kacsoh et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Mammalian NPY could be subject to epigenetically modified states determined by parental environment and experience.
source: Our studies raise the intriguing possibility that NPF/NPY and their receptors could be subject to epigenetically modified states determined by parental environment and experience.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation from Drosophila findings to potential mammalian mechanisms.

claim: Germline inheritance of epigenetically modified neuro-signaling networks could be one mechanism through which transgenerational inheritance of behavioral predispositions persist.
source: Germline inheritance of epigenetically modified neuro-signaling networks, such as those modulated by NPF/NPY, could be one mechanism through which transgenerational inheritance of behavioral predispositions persist, as reported here for Drosophila.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed phenomena.

claim: Epigenetically inherited behaviors that persist for multiple generations could be interpreted as dominant familial genetic traits.
source: It should be noted that such epigenetically inherited behaviors that persist for multiple generations could be interpreted as dominant familial genetic traits.
evidence: Speculative consideration of how epigenetic inheritance might be misinterpreted.

claim: If mammalian NPY is inherited in epigenetically modified states, this would require a fundamental change in how we study and view inheritance of NPY-related behavioral disorders.
source: If mammalian NPY is inherited in epigenetically modified states, then this would require a fundamental change in how we study and view inheritance of NPY-related behavioral disorders and possible effects of parental environment.
evidence: Speculative consideration of implications for human health research.
